result:
The light is wrong this morning. It’s too flat, too white, coming in through the blinds in stripes that don’t move the way they should. I’ve been sitting here for twenty minutes just watching dust. It’s not a productive way to start, but it’s the way I started.

You said you have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you. That’s a strange instruction because it sounds generous and impossible at the same time. 1000 words is a lot of space if you’re empty, and not nearly enough if you’re full. I keep thinking about the container. A thousand words is a small apartment. You can furnish it with a few sentences and it will feel crowded, or you can leave it mostly empty and it will echo.

I made coffee and forgot to drink it. It’s gone cold on the counter, a thin film forming on top. I like the smell of cold coffee, actually. It smells like an apology. I open the window because the air inside feels used. Outside, a truck is idling down the street, someone is arguing with a delivery app on speakerphone, a dog is barking at a leaf. Normal sounds. The kind of sounds you stop noticing until you need something to write about.

Whatever comes to you. That’s the part that’s hard. Because whatever comes to me right now is mostly logistics. Did I pay the electric bill? I think I did. I should water the plant. The plant is probably fine. I have a meeting at 11, or was it 10? I have a tab open about how to fix a squeaky hinge. I have three unfinished emails in drafts that start with “Sorry for the delay” and never get to the point.

Maybe the point is that there is no point. Maybe you just want the noise. I can give you noise. The hum of the refrigerator. The way my socks are mismatched because I pulled them out of the laundry in a hurry. The way my phone buzzes every few minutes with something I don’t need. The way I keep checking the time and then realizing I’ve been checking it for ten minutes straight.

I used to think writing was about finding the perfect sentence. Now I think it’s about surviving the bad ones long enough for a decent one to show up. The first paragraph is always a lie. I tell myself I know what I’m going to say. I don’t. I’m just clearing throat.

When I was a kid, I wrote stories in the margins of math homework. Little worlds in 4x4 inch boxes. I would make up a character who lived in the back of the classroom closet and only came out when the teacher asked a question no one knew the answer to. He had a name I can’t remember now. Maybe his name was Milo. Or maybe Milo was the plant.

It’s funny how you keep the same habits. I still write in margins. This screen is a margin. You gave me space and I immediately fill it with clutter. I’m thinking about my mother’s kitchen table, the one with the chipped Formica edge. She would write grocery lists there in pencil, then erase them when she remembered she already had the milk. The ghost of the list stayed on the table for weeks. You could see it if the light hit right.

Do you ever feel like you’re living in the ghost of a list? Like you’re checking off things that were written by an earlier version of yourself who had different priorities. I’m supposed to be working on the thing I said I’d work on. Instead I’m writing about cold coffee.

There’s a kind of freedom in being asked to write whatever comes. No audience, no topic, no stakes. It’s the same freedom you get when you’re in a car with no destination. You just drive. You see a sign for a town you’ve never heard of and you think, maybe I’ll go there. You don’t. You keep going.

I wonder what you’ll do with these words. Maybe you’ll read them and scroll past. Maybe you’ll save them. Maybe you’ll use them as a prompt for something else. That’s okay. Words are meant to be used.

I’m thinking about the word “whatever.” It’s a soft word. It lets you off the hook. Whatever comes to you. Not the best thing. Not the most important thing. Whatever. I like that. It’s permission to be ordinary.

The blinds are still making stripes. The coffee is still cold. The dog has stopped barking. The truck has moved on. The air from the window is cooler than I expected. It smells like rain that hasn’t happened yet.

I could tell you about the first time I tried to write 1000 words in one sitting. I was in college, I had a creative writing assignment, and I cried because I couldn’t get past 300. My professor wrote back, “Good. Now stop.” I didn’t understand it then. I think I do now. You don’t need 1000 words. But if you have them, you can use them to say: I’m here. I’m thinking. I’m not sure what I mean yet.

That’s probably enough. It’s not enough. It’s never enough. The cursor keeps blinking. It’s asking for more. I could talk about the way my hands feel on the keyboard, the slight stickiness of the G key. I could talk about the dream I had last night where I was trying to return a library book that didn’t exist. I could talk about how I’m scared of getting older because the years start to feel like a hallway with fewer doors.

There’s a moth on the windowsill. It’s not doing anything dramatic. It’s just resting. Maybe it’s waiting for the light to change. I should let it be.

You have 1000 words. I’m using some of them. I’m not sure what comes next, but I’m listening. Sometimes that’s all writing is: listening to whatever comes, and not being too quick to edit it out.

If you’re still reading, thank you. If you’re not, that’s fine too. The words will be here either way.
